title: Same question, every model: cross-model scenario battery
about: Battery run on 6 Nov 2026 on the hosted PolicyEngine Macro MCP (adapter 0.2.0). Cells with a stored path were fetched for this file; cells marked 'battery' are the values from the same day's battery (macro#213), stored with their exact call. Committed cells are read from a model repository's own outputs, with no solve. Regenerate the FRB/US cells with models/compare/run_battery.py --refresh frb-us.

boe-1999.label: Bank of England, 1pp rise held one year
boe-1999.text: Output −0.2% to −0.35% after about a year; inflation −0.2 to −0.4pp a year or so after that. 1pp × 4 quarters = 4 pp-quarters, so 0.05–0.09% of GDP per pp-quarter.
boe-1999.source: Bank of England, The transmission mechanism of monetary policy, Quarterly Bulletin 1999 Q2

fed-2018.label: Fed FRB/US, 100bp funds-rate shock (VAR expectations), current model
fed-2018.text: The Board's own simulation of the current (post-2018) model: output gap trough −0.486pp, core PCE inflation trough −0.0345pp and unemployment peak +0.219pp, all at quarter 8. The previous model gives −0.459pp, −0.062pp and +0.215pp. The −0.4pp and −0.08pp in the 2014 FEDS Note describe the pre-2018 model.
fed-2018.gdp_units: pp output gap, trough, current and previous model
fed-2018.source: Laforte, Overview of the changes to the FRB/US model (2018), FEDS Notes, 7 Dec 2018, doi:10.17016/2380-7172.2306, Fig. 2 (accessible data table)

purchases.label: Purchases multiplier, year 1
purchases.text: CBO 0.45–1.82 (Fed responding); Ramey 2019 0.6–1; Coenen et al. 2012 FRB-US, no accommodation, ≈0.95. OBR uses 0.6 for current spending on impact, tapering to zero over five years (OBR, Nov 2023).
purchases.source: Whalen and Reichling, CBO Working Paper 2015-02 (converted); Ramey, Journal of Economic Perspectives 2019; Coenen et al., AEJ: Macroeconomics 2012; OBR, Dynamic scoring of policy measures in OBR forecasts, Nov 2023

tax.label: Tax multiplier
tax.text: CBO, Fed not tightening: two-year lower/middle-income cut 0.3–1.5; one-year higher-income cut 0.1–0.6; no central value. OBR household tax 0.3 on impact, decaying.
tax.source: Whalen and Reichling, CBO Working Paper 2015-02; OBR, Dynamic scoring of policy measures in OBR forecasts, Nov 2023

questions.title: What does a 100bp rise in the policy rate do?
questions.experiment: A 1pp rise in the policy rate. The models do not share a rate path, so each row states its own and the size of the path in pp-quarters (annualised rate × quarters).
notes: GDP per pp-quarter divides the peak GDP effect by the rate path's size to the peak. HANK's figure uses the realised real-rate path; the other rows use the nominal policy rate, which is close to the real rate in FRB/US because its inflation barely moves. On HANK's rstar path (10 pp-quarters at ρ = 0.9) the figure would be about 0.04%, so HANK's 0.16 and FRB/US's 0.15 are not like-for-like.
HANK reports inflation as a quarterly rate; this page multiplies it by 4 to give an annual rate.

short.why: GDP 3–6× below the BoE range; prices flat

cells.timing: GDP peaks at q4; no price response
cells.reason: GDP is 3–6× below the BoE 1999 range (−0.2% to −0.35%), through consumption only; inflation and unemployment are exactly zero.

short.why: 4.6–8× the BoE peak; 2–4× per pp-quarter

args.shock: 1 s.d. UK monetary-policy shock (+25bp on impact), scaled ×4

cells.rate_path: +25bp on impact, still +0.17pp at h = 12 (a unit root: the rate does not revert); about 1.9 pp-quarters to h = 8 per 25bp

gdp.units: % of GDP, at h = 8, scaled from −0.39% per 25bp

inflation.units: % on the CPI level at h = 20, scaled from −0.63% per 25bp

cells.timing: GDP −0.14% per s.d. on impact, building to −0.39% by h = 8; no reversion within 5 years
cells.reason: At h = 8 GDP is −1.6% (scaled to 100bp) against the BoE's −0.2% to −0.35% after about a year: 4.6–8× the peak, or 2–4× per pp-quarter once the SVAR's longer rate path is allowed for. It builds to h = 8 and does not revert within 5 years (the rate path has a unit root), against the BoE's fullest effect after about a year.
cells.draws: The medians are from the repository's fast test fixture (600 posterior draws, about 50 accepted, unweighted; tests/conftest.py), not the published replication run (10,000 draws, 765 accepted, effective sample size 368.0; results/summary.md at c827ab8). An earlier sense check found bands wider than the paper's (186 accepted draws, effective sample size 91, against the paper's 10,000; results/sense_check.md).

short.why: Core PCE matches; unemployment 1.04× on the Board's design

run.label: local run at frbus 162cfe6 (October 2026 LONGBASE), 2026-11-18, shocks from 2026Q3 (the first quarter after LONGBASE history)

cells.rate_path: +1.00pp on impact, decays under the inertial rule, crosses zero at q8, undershoots
cells.timing: Hump: GDP and inflation peak at q8
cells.verdict_label: Plausible; within 10% of the Board on its own design
cells.reason: The Board's simulation of the current model gives an output-gap trough of −0.486pp, core PCE −0.0345pp and an unemployment peak of +0.219pp at quarter 8 (Laforte 2018). This run gives core PCE −0.034pp at quarter 8 and an output-gap trough of −0.50pp, and an unemployment peak of +0.28pp, 1.28× the Board's. That ratio depends on the start date: on the Board's own 2020Q1 design the model gives +0.228pp, 1.04×, with core PCE 0.96× and the output gap 0.97× (us-frb-model results/inflation_transmission.md at 162cfe6). The −0.08pp in earlier Fed notes describes the pre-2018 model.

short.why: Inflation peaks on impact, not after two years

cells.rate_path: Taylor-rule intercept shock (rstar) +0.25pp a quarter, AR(1) ρ = 0.9: not a policy-rate rise of that size. The nominal policy rate the rule sets falls 0.25pp a quarter on impact (about 1.0pp annualised), because inflation falls by more than the intercept rises (i = rstar + 1.5π), and is still 0.11pp below steady state at q11. Realised real rate +1.36pp annualised on impact
cells.timing: Both peak on impact; no hump
cells.verdict_label: Plausible in-model, off on timing; an intercept shock, not a 100bp rate rise
cells.reason: Inflation is about 40× FRB/US and 3–7× the BoE range, and peaks on impact rather than after about two years, which is consistent with the model's forward-looking Phillips curve. The shock is to the rule's intercept: the nominal policy rate falls while the real rate rises.

questions.title: What does government spending of 1% of GDP do to output?
questions.experiment: Higher government purchases worth about 1% of GDP. The multiplier is the GDP change divided by the spending change, both in % of GDP. Financing and the monetary rule differ by model and drive most of the spread.
notes: FRB/US's hosted tool cannot run a sustained +1%-of-GDP experiment: the stored run is a one-quarter impulse of about 0.046% of GDP, and the year-1 figure comes from a committed sustained run (macro #212).

short.why: An accounting identity; the OBR's own figure is 0.6

cells.experiment: CGG +£7,000m a quarter (about 1.0% of GDP) for 4 quarters

gdp.units: % of GDP, peak (+1.007% to +1.017% over q1–q4, +0.02% at q5, fading)

cells.solver: converged in all 12 quarters (nominal-GDP pin); the tool's own caveat calls the result an upper bound
cells.reason: 1.01→1.03 comes from an identity, not estimated behaviour. It falls inside CBO's range but sits above Ramey's upper bound of 1 and the OBR's own 0.6.
The BoE SVAR identifies no fiscal shock.

short.why: 0.81 impact, 0.747 yr 1: inside both ranges

run.label: local run at frbus 162cfe6 (October 2026 LONGBASE), 2026-11-18, shocks from 2026Q3 (the first quarter after LONGBASE history)

cells.experiment: Federal purchases +1% (about 0.046% of GDP), one quarter

gdp.units: % of GDP, peak, per 0.046% of GDP spent

cells.multiplier: about 0.81 on impact; 0.747 in year 1 for a committed sustained run from 2026Q1 (inertial rule; us-frb-model results/benchmark_multipliers.md)
cells.reason: Impact 0.81 and year-1 0.747 sit inside CBO's 0.45–1.82 and Ramey's 0.6–1. Both are below Coenen's ≈0.95, which is consistent: Coenen assumes no accommodation, while this run uses an inertial Taylor rule that responds.

short.why: Sign flips while spending is still high

cells.experiment: G +1% of GDP on impact, AR(1) ρ = 0.8, financed by the labour tax
cells.multiplier: 0.175 (ρ = 0.8); 0.075 at ρ = 0.9. Output turns negative from q3 while spending is still 51–73% of impact
cells.reason: Impact 0.175 at ρ 0.8 is below the CBO floor of 0.45 and Ramey's floor of 0.6. Labour-tax financing differs from the benchmark setups, so it cannot be ruled off.

short.why: Annual, investment-led; not comparable

cells.multiplier: 2.25 nominal per £ of the power-sector spending the policy sets, from the 2027 policy start to 2040; back-loaded: 0.47 after one year, 0.79 to 2031, 1.40 to 2034. Over the full run from 2023: 2.30 nominal (3.26 in real terms: real ΔGDP 250.6 over deflated spending of 76.8), and 1.78 per £ of all non-wage spending. Parameter mismatch included: 2.25 if its effect stops in 2027, as low as 2.08 if it persists (1.73–1.75 for the secondary)
cells.reason: The headline impulse is now the policy instrument, government power-sector spending (define-uk-model #16, decided 15 Nov 2026). An annual, investment-led scenario cumulated to 2040 is still not comparable to a 4-quarter purchases shock, and the published comparators (the OBR's impact multiplier of about 1.0; Batini et al. 2021, IMF WP/21/87: 1.1–1.5 for renewable investment) are short-horizon, where this model sits below them (0.47 after one year). Both figures include a Baseline/policy parameter mismatch (define-uk-model #20).

questions.title: What does a 1pp rise in the personal tax rate do?
questions.experiment: A rise in the effective personal income-tax rate of about 1pp.
notes: FRB/US with periods = 4 stacks the tax add-factor to +2.37pp rather than +1pp, and the tool's label does not warn (macro #212). The stored run uses periods = 1.

short.why: Rises where the OBR's 0.3 decays

cells.multiplier: 0.21 at q4, rising to 0.38 by q12, in current prices, the basis of the OBR's 0.3 and of the Overview (0.19 and 0.33 in real GDP)
cells.reason: Right order of magnitude, but it rises where the OBR's 0.3 decays.
The BoE SVAR identifies no tax shock.
